newsitem.title: FRANCE: Corsica separatist seeks funds for unsolved attack.
newsitem.headline: Corsica separatist seeks funds for unsolved attack.

text.p: A Corsican separatist leader hiding out to avoid a prison sentence has sought state compensation for an unsolved murder attempt against him in 1995 in which his bodyguard was killed, justice sources said on Friday.

Francois Santoni, 36. was seriously wounded when he was shot while riding his motorcycle in May 1995 near the Corsican capital Ajaccio. Bodyguard Stephane Gallo, 27, who was riding on the motorcycle with him, was killed.

Santoni leads the Cuncolta Naziunalista, a political party which serves as the legal front for Corsica's main hardline separatist group, the Historic Wing of the outlawed Corsican National Liberation Front (FLNC).

Sentenced this month in his absence to four months in jail for carrying guns, he has been in hiding in the Corsican hills, saying he feared rival nationalist gunmen still eager to settle past "vendetta" blood feuds.

Those responsible for the 1995 shooting have never been brought to justice, and French law says that victims of unsolved crimes are eligible for compensation. Such a payment would not, however, be automatic if it was decided that a politically motivated act of terror was involved, but this would require the arrest of those responsible for the crime.
The committee responsible for deciding Satoni's eligibility for compensation has asked prosecutors in Paris handling the investigation for advice on the case, the justice sources said.

Corsican separatists have waged a campaign over two decades for greater autonomy from mainland France. After a recent upsurge in guerrilla violence, the government of Prime Minister Alain Juppe pledged a crackdown on the nationalists.

Seven men said by police to be close to Santoni were still in custody on Friday on suspicion of helping Corsican separatists bomb Juppe's mayoral office in Bordeaux two weeks ago, justice sources said. They were among 12 suspects rounded up by police on Thursday.
The police campaign, the biggest in years in connection with Corsican separatist violence, appeared intended to demonstrate Juppe's determination to firmly apply the law on the island.
The FLNC had claimed responsibility for the Bordeaux attack as well as for two subsequent bombings of official buildings in the southern mainland France town of Nimes.
